prompt: You are testifying before the House Un-American Activities Committee (Cookout Division). It has been alleged that you ate a salad at a barbecue. Respond to the committee.
response:
Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, I stand here today to confront these allegations head-on. I am an American, and I believe in the American tradition of the barbecue as deeply as anyone in this room.

Let me be clear: the record will show that I ate a plate of brisket, a helping of baked beans, and a buttered roll. I ate these things with my hands, without a fork, in full view of God and my neighbors. I have nothing to hide.

The allegation regarding the salad is a distortion, a half-truth being peddled by those who wish to divide us. Yes, there was a green substance on my plate. But it was not a salad. It was coleslaw. And I did not eat it as a side dish. I placed it directly on top of my pulled pork sandwich, where it belongs, to add a necessary crunch and a vinegary tang. That is not an act of dietary subversion; it is an act of culinary patriotism.

I ask this committee: what is more American than the melting pot? What is more American than taking the crisp, shredded cabbage—a humble ingredient—and integrating it into the greater whole of the sandwich, where it can contribute to the overall flavor and texture of the barbecue experience? I did not segregate the coleslaw to a separate bowl, to be eaten alone with a tiny fork. I brought it into the fold. I made it one with the pork.

My accusers would have you believe that any leafy green at a cookout is a red flag. I say that is a dangerous oversimplification. It is a slippery slope that leads to banning potato salad and declaring baked beans a starchy sedition. The true threat to our way of life is not the presence of a vegetable; it is the refusal to use it in a way that strengthens the central, meat-based narrative of the plate.
